### Stage: items

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
At a school, pupils who signed up for a reading programme are randomly assigned: 60 to the programme and 60 to a comparison group. All 120 pupils take the same reading test at the start and at the end of the term. At the end, 20 pupils in the programme group, all with low start scores, have left the programme and do not take the final test. In the comparison group, 2 pupils are missing. The programme group's average score is higher than the comparison group's.

Which threat to internal validity most directly weakens the conclusion that the programme caused this difference?

A. Selection, because the two groups differed before the programme started.
B. Attrition, because mainly weak readers left the programme group.
C. Testing, because pupils took the same reading test twice.
D. Maturation, because reading skills grow naturally during a term.

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A teacher gives all 90 pupils in year 2 a spelling test. She selects the 12 pupils with the lowest scores and gives them extra support for six weeks. Then these 12 pupils take a different, equally difficult spelling test. Their average score has risen. No other pupils are tested again.

Which threat to internal validity, linked to how these 12 pupils were chosen, could explain part of the rise even if the extra support had no effect?

A. History, because events at school during the six weeks may have helped the pupils.
B. Testing, because the pupils had already done a spelling test before.
C. Selection, because the 12 pupils are not equivalent to the other pupils.
D. Regression to the mean, because pupils with very low scores tend to score closer to average again.

### Question 3 (1 pt)
Researchers recruit 40 first-year psychology students for a study in a quiet university lab. Students are randomly assigned to learn vocabulary with a new flashcard app or with a paper list. Both groups take the same vocabulary test afterwards, and all 40 students complete the study. The app group remembers more words. The researchers conclude that the app will also improve vocabulary learning for secondary-school pupils in busy classrooms.

Which problem most directly limits this conclusion?

A. The results may not generalise to other people and settings.
B. Random assignment may have failed to create equivalent groups.
C. Uneven drop-out may have made the groups different by the end.
D. The measurement of vocabulary may have differed between the groups.

### Question 4 (1 pt)
A school wants to know whether a new feedback method improves essay quality. In October, one teacher scores all pupils' essays with a detailed rubric on a 10-point scale. The method is used for one term. In February, a different teacher scores new essays from the same pupils with a shorter rubric on a 5-point scale. Both sets of scores are converted to percentages. The February percentages are higher.

Which threat to internal validity is created by the way the essays were scored?

A. Testing, because pupils practised writing essays in October.
B. Maturation, because pupils' writing improves naturally over a term.
C. Instrumentation, because the way of scoring changed between the measurements.
D. History, because something else happened at school during the term.

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A researcher wants to know whether a mentoring programme reduced drop-out among the 200 first-year vocational students who took part in a study. A lottery assigns 100 students to mentoring and 100 to no mentoring. Drop-out is recorded for both groups after one year, in the same way.

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. It cannot answer the question, because there is no pretest to check that the groups were equal.
B. It cannot answer the question, because students who volunteer are not representative of all students.
C. It can answer the question, because random assignment controls selection.
D. It can answer the question only if the groups are first matched on age and gender.

### Question 6 (1 pt)
A municipality introduces a homework-support scheme in all its primary schools in January. An adviser measures the school wellbeing of the same 300 pupils in September and again in June. Wellbeing scores are higher in June. The adviser asks: did the scheme raise pupils' wellbeing?

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. It can answer the question, because the same pupils are measured twice, so differences between pupils are excluded.
B. It cannot answer the question, because other changes over time are not ruled out by this design.
C. It can answer the question, because the difference between September and June is statistically significant.
D. It cannot answer the question, because two measurements cannot show which came first, scheme or wellbeing.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
A researcher surveys a random sample of 500 pupils from 20 secondary schools. Each pupil reports the number of hours they sleep per night and gives their most recent maths grade. The correlation is positive: pupils who sleep more have higher grades. The researcher asks: does more sleep lead to higher grades?

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. It can answer the question, because a sample of 500 pupils is large enough to rule out other explanations.
B. It can answer the question, because a positive correlation shows that sleep comes before the grades.
C. It cannot answer the question, because self-reported sleep hours contain error, which makes any causal claim impossible.
D. It cannot answer the question, because the correlation does not show whether sleep affects grades or grades affect sleep.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
A school has two parallel classes. The principal decides that class 3A gets a peer-tutoring programme for one term and class 3B continues as usual. At the end of the term, a researcher gives both classes the same maths test, and 3A scores higher. The researcher wants to answer: did peer tutoring raise maths results? The classes were not formed at random.

Which addition would most improve this design's ability to answer the question?

A. A maths test in both classes before the programme, so that differences at the start can be taken into account.
B. A second maths test in both classes a month after the programme, so that lasting differences can be seen.
C. A questionnaire in class 3A asking pupils whether they found the programme useful.
D. A repeat of the study in another school with the same two-class set-up.

### Question 9 (1 pt)
A researcher wants to know whether a new digital feedback tool improves pupils' writing scores. 120 pupils in one school can take part, and the school lets the researcher decide who uses the tool.

Which design is best able to answer this causal question?

A. Ask all 120 pupils how often they use the tool and correlate this with their writing grades.
B. Let all 120 pupils use the tool and compare their writing scores before and after.
C. Randomly assign 60 pupils to the tool and 60 to usual teaching, then compare writing scores afterwards.
D. Let pupils choose whether to use the tool and compare users with non-users afterwards.

### Question 10 (1 pt)
A researcher measures the exam anxiety of 80 students before and after an eight-week mindfulness course. There is no other group. Anxiety is lower after the course. The researcher wants to be able to say whether the course caused the decrease, separate from other changes over time.

Which change to the design does this best?

A. Measure anxiety with a questionnaire that is more reliable and valid.
B. Add more students to the course group so that the sample is larger.
C. Add a second posttest some weeks after the first posttest.
D. Add a control group that is randomly assigned and measured at the same times.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Understand (questions 1–4)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. The weakest readers left only the programme group, so the remaining programme pupils score higher on average because of who stayed. This is differential drop-out, which is attrition.
**A:** Wrong because pupils were randomly assigned, so the groups were equivalent at the start. The distractor catches students who see unequal groups at the end and call it selection.
**C:** Wrong because both groups took the same test twice, so any testing effect applies to both groups and does not explain the difference. It catches students who name a threat that is present in the case but is not the main one.
**D:** Wrong because natural growth during the term affects both groups. It catches students who name maturation for any change over time.

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** D. The 12 pupils were chosen for their extreme low scores, so they are likely to score closer to average on a retest without any effect of the support.
**A:** Wrong because history is not tied to how the pupils were chosen, and the case gives no sign of such an event. It catches students who name history for any change over time without a control group.
**B:** Wrong because the retest used a different, equally difficult test, which removes the effect of repeating the same test. It catches students who think any retest causes a testing effect.
**C:** Wrong because selection concerns non-equivalent groups that are compared. No comparison is made here, and selection does not create a rise on its own. It catches a mix-up between selecting extreme pupils (regression) and non-equivalent groups (selection).

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. The sample (first-year psychology students) and the setting (quiet lab) differ from the target (secondary-school pupils in busy classrooms), which is a threat to external validity.
**B:** Wrong because random assignment controls selection, so the groups were equivalent at the start. It catches the misconception that randomisation can fail by definition or is not enough.
**C:** Wrong because all 40 students completed the study, so there was no drop-out. It catches students who pick an internal threat from the list.
**D:** Wrong because both groups took the same vocabulary test, so measurement did not change. It catches students who pick an internal threat from the list.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. Different scorers, rubrics and scales were used in October and February, so a change in measurement may explain the difference. This is instrumentation.
**A:** Wrong because the case describes a change in scoring, not an effect of the earlier measurement. It catches students who name testing for any repeated measurement.
**B:** Wrong because maturation is a real threat in this one-group design, but it is not created by the way the essays were scored, which is what the question asks.
**D:** Wrong because history is a general threat in this design, but it is not created by the way the essays were scored, which is what the question asks.

### Row R2 — Evaluate (questions 5–10)

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** C. Random assignment (the lottery) controls selection, so the design supports a causal claim about the students who took part.
**A:** Wrong because randomisation makes the groups equivalent without needing a pretest to establish it. It catches the belief that a pretest is always required for a causal claim.
**B:** Wrong because representativeness concerns external validity (generalising), not whether the effect among these students is caused by the programme. The question is about the participating students only. It catches a mix-up of internal and external validity.
**D:** Wrong because random assignment already controls selection, so matching is not needed. It catches the belief that groups must be matched in addition to randomisation.

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** B. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression to the mean, so it cannot show that the scheme raised wellbeing.
**A:** Wrong because measuring the same pupils twice does not rule out events or natural change between the two measurements. It catches the belief that using the same persons solves all validity problems.
**C:** Wrong because statistical significance shows that a difference is unlikely to be chance, not what caused it. It catches a mix-up of statistical significance and causal inference.
**D:** Wrong because the scheme started before the June measurement, so the order of events is known. The problem is the alternative explanations. It catches a mix-up with the correlational design, which cannot establish direction.

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** D. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so grades could also influence sleep.
**A:** Wrong because sample size does not control for explanations or establish direction. It catches the belief that a large sample makes a causal claim possible.
**B:** Wrong because a correlation does not show which variable comes first. It catches the belief that a strong correlation implies causation.
**C:** Wrong because measurement error makes results less precise but does not make every causal claim impossible, and it is not the weakness the material names for this design. It catches a mix-up with instrumentation and an overstated claim about measurement error.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** A. A quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups needs a pretest and control for selection, so a pretest in both classes lets the researcher take the differences at the start into account.
**B:** Wrong because a later test shows whether the difference lasts but does not address the non-equivalent classes. It catches students who add more measurements instead of controlling selection.
**C:** Wrong because opinions of pupils in one class do not show the programme's effect on results and do not control selection. It catches students who accept satisfaction as evidence of effect.
**D:** Wrong because repeating the same set-up repeats the selection problem. At best it relates to generalisation. It catches a mix-up of replication or external validity with internal validity.

#### Question 9
**Correct answer:** C. A randomised controlled trial supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection, and here the researcher can decide who uses the tool.
**A:** Wrong because a correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect. It catches the belief that correlating use with grades answers a causal question.
**B:** Wrong because a one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression to the mean. It catches the belief that a before–after difference shows the effect.
**D:** Wrong because pupils who choose to use the tool may differ from those who do not, so selection is not controlled. It catches the belief that having a comparison group is enough.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** D. A randomly assigned control group measured at the same times faces the same history, maturation and regression, so the course effect can be separated from other changes over time.
**A:** Wrong because a better questionnaire improves measurement but does not separate the course effect from other changes over time. It catches the belief that measurement quality solves design problems.
**B:** Wrong because a larger sample does not control history, maturation or regression. It catches the belief that more participants strengthen a causal claim.
**C:** Wrong because a second posttest adds a measurement but no comparison, so other changes over time are still not ruled out. It catches the belief that more measurements in one group can show causation.

## Check against the blueprint

| Row | Planned | Written | Questions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | 4 | 4 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| R2 | 6 | 6 | 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 |
| Total | 10 questions, 10 points | 10 questions, 10 points | 1–10 |

Correct answers by position: A = 2 (questions 3, 8), B = 2 (questions 1, 6), C = 3 (questions 4, 5, 9), D = 3 (questions 2, 7, 10).

Remarks:
- I found no error in the blueprint.
- Coverage in R1: four questions cannot cover all seven internal threats plus external validity. The correct answers cover attrition, regression to the mean, external validity and instrumentation. Selection, history, maturation and testing appear as distractors only.
- Coverage in R2: randomised controlled trial (questions 5, 9), quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups (question 8), one-group pretest–posttest (questions 6, 10), correlational design (question 7).

## Self-check

- **Does every multiple-choice question have exactly one correct answer?** Yes, because each case rules out the other options with facts in the stem (for example random assignment, a different equivalent test, full completion) or with the material (for example direction in correlational designs).
- **Is there no clue to the correct answer anywhere?** Yes, because I kept the options in each question alike in length and form, and the correct answers are spread over A to D.
- **Are all distractors plausible?** Yes, because each one is a known mix-up, such as internal versus external validity, pretest–posttest versus correlational, or a large sample versus control of selection.
- **Does every question test the cognitive level of its row?** Yes, because questions 1–4 ask students to classify a threat in a new case (Understand) and questions 5–10 ask for a judgement of a design against causal inference in a new case (Evaluate).
- **Does everything follow from the material?** Yes, because all threats, designs and judgements come from the material, and all case data are fictitious and given in full in each question.
- **Does any question give away the answer to another?** No, because each case is separate, and the one-group design in questions 6 and 10 is approached from different sides without naming the control-group solution in question 6.

### Stage: blueprint

## Link to the learning outcomes

- **Outcome 1: The student identifies threats to internal and external validity in a described study.** Cognitive level: Apply. The student uses the known threat categories on a new, described study. This is not a Remember question, because the case is not an example from the material. No lower-level prerequisite question is included.
- **Outcome 2: The student evaluates whether a described research design can answer a given causal research question.** Cognitive level: Evaluate. The student judges the design against criteria (internal validity, control of selection, direction of effect) and justifies a conclusion about the causal question. Multiple choice can test this with a new case.

## Test blueprint

| Row | Learning outcome | Cognitive level | Question type | Number of questions | Points per question | Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Identify threats to internal and external validity in a described study | Apply | Multiple choice | 4 | 1 | 4 |
| R2 | Evaluate whether a research design can answer a causal research question | Evaluate | Multiple choice | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| Total | | | | 10 | | 10 |

## Distribution and points

- **Total:** 10 questions at 1 point each gives 10 points. This comes from the teacher.
- **Outcome 1 (R1):** 4 points, 40% of the total. Proposal.
- **Outcome 2 (R2):** 6 points, 60% of the total. Proposal. The teacher gave no weighting. I weighted outcome 2 more heavily because it asks for a higher cognitive process and covers four designs, each needing its own judgement.
- **Test duration:** 45 minutes, from the teacher. Time estimate (Proposal), based on case-based multiple choice with a short case text:
  - R1: 4 questions × about 2.5 minutes = about 10 minutes.
  - R2: 6 questions × about 3.5 minutes = about 21 minutes.
  - Total: about 31 minutes, which leaves about 14 minutes for reading, checking and a margin. The test fits in 45 minutes.
- **Pass mark:** the teacher gave none, so none is set here.
- **Coverage within the rows (Proposal for step 2):** R1 should cover both internal threats (selection, history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, attrition) and external threats (unrepresentative sample, artificial setting). R2 should cover the four designs in the material: randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups, one-group pretest–posttest, and correlational design. Every question needs a new case that does not appear literally in the material.

## Self-check

- **Does the blueprint add up?** Yes. The questions are 4 + 6 = 10, and the points are 4 + 6 = 10, which matches the teacher's total of 10 points at 1 point per question.
- **Does every outcome get tested at the level of its verb?** Yes. R1 tests Apply and R2 tests Evaluate, and neither goes beyond what its verb asks.
- **Does every outcome included have at least two questions?** Yes. Outcome 1 has 4 questions and outcome 2 has 6.
- **Does every question type fit its cognitive level?** Yes. Multiple choice can test Apply with a case, and Evaluate with a case, and the teacher allows only multiple choice.

### Stage: items

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
A school tests a new writing course. In September, Ms Jansen grades all students' essays. In December, after the course, Mr Bakker grades the essays because Ms Jansen is ill. He uses looser grading criteria. The students score higher in December.

Which threat to internal validity is introduced by the way the essays were graded?

A. Testing
B. Instrumentation
C. Maturation
D. History

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A school gives all 200 first-year students a maths test in October. The 20 students with the lowest scores join extra tutoring. In January, these 20 students take a different maths test of equal difficulty. Their average score is higher than in October.

Which threat to internal validity follows directly from how these students were selected?

A. Maturation
B. Testing
C. Regression to the mean
D. History

### Question 3 (1 pt)
A company randomly assigns 100 employees to a stress-reduction course (50) or a waiting list (50). After six months, 20 employees in the course group have left the study, mostly people who found the course too demanding because of their high workload. Only 2 employees in the waiting-list group have left. The remaining course participants report lower stress than the waiting-list group.

Which threat to internal validity does this describe?

A. Attrition
B. Selection
C. Instrumentation
D. History

### Question 4 (1 pt)
Researchers test a feedback app that is meant for regular classrooms. They randomly select 400 students from schools across the country and randomly assign them to the app or to a control condition. Each student works alone in a quiet university lab room, with a researcher watching. The app group scores higher. The researchers conclude that the app also works in regular classrooms.

Which threat to external validity is the most important problem for this conclusion?

A. Unrepresentative sample
B. Selection
C. Artificial setting
D. Instrumentation

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A municipality gives the pupils of one primary school a free breakfast for a year. Absence rates in the year before (pretest) and the year after (posttest) are compared. The absence rate fell. A policy adviser wants to know whether the free breakfast caused the fall.

Which evaluation of this design is correct?

A. It can answer the question, because the same pupils are measured twice, so other explanations are ruled out.
B. It can answer the question, because a fall after the breakfast started shows the breakfast caused it.
C. It cannot answer the question, because other events or natural change during the year could also explain the fall.
D. It cannot answer the question, because pupils were not randomly assigned, so selection explains the fall.

### Question 6 (1 pt)
A survey among 300 students at one college measures weekly use of a study-planning app and each student's grade average. Students who use the app more have higher grades. A policy adviser concludes: "The app raises grades, so we should require its use."

Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

A. It is justified, because a clear correlation shows that the app causes higher grades.
B. It is not justified, because the direction is unknown: students with high grades may use the app more.
C. It is not justified, because a correlational design cannot show any relationship between two variables.
D. It is not justified, because the survey has no pretest, so regression to the mean explains the correlation.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
A teacher wants to know whether a new peer-tutoring programme improves reading scores. She gives the programme to her own class (class 1). She does not give it to a parallel class (class 2), which she picked because it looked similar. At the end of the term, only a reading test is taken. Class 1 scores higher than class 2.

Can this design answer the causal question?

A. No, because differences between the classes before the programme could explain the posttest difference.
B. Yes, because comparing with a control class rules out all threats to internal validity.
C. Yes, because the teacher knows the classes well and so picked comparable ones.
D. No, because with only one outcome measure the direction of the effect stays unclear.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
A municipality will offer a homework-support programme in two of its neighbourhoods. Random assignment of residents is not possible. A policy adviser must choose a design to find out whether the programme improves pupils' grades.

Which design is best able to answer this causal question?

A. Measure grades before and after the programme in the two neighbourhoods, without a comparison group.
B. Survey pupils in all neighbourhoods on programme use and grades, then correlate the two.
C. Compare grades after the programme in the two neighbourhoods with grades in two other neighbourhoods.
D. Measure grades before and after in the two neighbourhoods and in two other neighbourhoods, and control for pretest differences.

### Question 9 (1 pt)
Researchers randomly assign 200 pupils from several schools to a tutoring programme (100 pupils) or a control group (100 pupils). Both groups take the same test before and after the programme. No pupil dropped out. The tutoring group improves more. A reviewer asks whether this design can support the claim that tutoring caused the extra improvement for these pupils.

Which evaluation is correct?

A. No, because an experiment shows only that two variables are related, not which came first.
B. Yes, because random assignment controls selection, so the groups differ only by chance.
C. No, because causal claims need groups matched on pupil characteristics, which random assignment does not do.
D. No, because causal claims need a study in a natural setting, and an experiment does not provide one.

### Question 10 (1 pt)
Researchers randomly assign 120 volunteers from one private school to a tutoring programme or to a control group. The tutoring group scores higher. The authors conclude: "Tutoring improves results for all secondary-school pupils."

Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

A. It is justified, because random assignment makes the results generalise to all pupils.
B. It is not justified, because the use of volunteers means selection threatens internal validity.
C. The effect for these pupils is supported, but generalising to all pupils is not, because the sample is unrepresentative.
D. It is not justified, because a randomised design cannot show whether tutoring or something else caused the difference.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Apply (questions 1–4)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. The change of grader and criteria between pretest and posttest is a change in measurement, which is instrumentation.
**A:** Wrong. Testing is the effect of having taken a pretest. The case is about a different grader, not about practice. It catches students who see any pretest–posttest design as a testing problem.
**C:** Wrong. Maturation is natural change in the students over time. The question asks about a threat introduced by the grading. It catches students who name the most familiar threat for a before–after design.
**D:** Wrong. History is an outside event during the study. The case describes no such event, only a change in how essays were graded. It catches students who mix up "something changed" with "an event happened".

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** C. The students were selected because they scored extremely low, so their scores are expected to move towards the average on a retest even without tutoring.
**A:** Wrong. Maturation is natural development over time. The question asks which threat follows from the way the students were selected, and that is extreme scores. It catches students who think any improvement without a control group is maturation.
**B:** Wrong. A different test of equal difficulty was used, so practice from the pretest is not the issue. It catches students who see "tested twice" and name testing.
**D:** Wrong. The case names no outside event. It catches students who treat "time passed between two measurements" as history.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. Many more people left the course group than the waiting-list group, and the leavers were those with high workload. This is differential drop-out, which is attrition.
**B:** Wrong. Selection is non-equivalent groups at the start. Here the groups were randomly assigned, so the problem arose later through drop-out. It catches students who confuse unequal groups at the end with unequal groups at the start.
**C:** Wrong. Nothing in the case says the way stress was measured changed. It catches students who think any biased outcome is a measurement problem.
**D:** Wrong. The case names no outside event during the six months. It catches students who pick a threat by its general sound instead of by the case.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. Working alone in a lab with a researcher watching differs from a regular classroom, so this is an artificial setting.
**A:** Wrong. The students were randomly selected from schools across the country, so the sample is not the problem. It catches students who assume every generalisation problem is a sample problem.
**B:** Wrong. Selection is an internal validity threat, and random assignment controls it here. The question asks about external validity. It catches students who mix up internal and external threats.
**D:** Wrong. Instrumentation is an internal validity threat and nothing in the case suggests a change in measurement. It catches the same mix-up of internal and external threats.

### Row R2 — Evaluate (questions 5–10)

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** C. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression, so other events or natural change could explain the fall.
**A:** Wrong. Measuring the same pupils twice does not rule out other explanations. It catches students who think a pretest controls everything.
**B:** Wrong. A change after an intervention does not prove the intervention caused it; this is the "after, so because" error. History and maturation remain possible.
**D:** Wrong. With one group there are no two groups to be non-equivalent, so selection is not the problem. The real problems are history, maturation and regression. It catches students who equate "no random assignment" with "selection explains the result".

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** B. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so higher grades could lead to more app use.
**A:** Wrong. A correlation alone does not show cause or direction. It catches the common mistake of reading a clear correlation as proof of cause.
**C:** Wrong. A correlational design can show that two variables are related. It cannot show direction. It catches students who overstate the limit of correlational research.
**D:** Wrong. Regression to the mean concerns the selection of extreme groups and a later measurement. It does not explain a correlation in a single survey. It catches students who mix up threat concepts.

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** A. The class was chosen by the teacher and there is no pretest, so differences that existed before the programme (selection) could explain the posttest difference.
**B:** Wrong. A comparison class does not rule out all threats. Without random assignment or a pretest, selection remains. It catches students who think any control group makes a design causal.
**C:** Wrong. The teacher's judgement that the classes look similar is not a control for selection. A pretest and control for selection are needed. It catches students who trust informal matching.
**D:** Wrong. The number of outcome measures is not the issue, and the problem is not the direction of the effect. That limit belongs to correlational designs. It catches students who mix up the limits of different designs.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** D. A quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups needs a pretest and control for selection, and option D has both plus a comparison group.
**A:** Wrong. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression. It catches students who think a pretest alone is enough.
**B:** Wrong. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect. It catches students who think a large survey can answer a causal question.
**C:** Wrong. A comparison group without a pretest cannot show whether the neighbourhoods already differed (selection). It catches students who think a comparison group alone is enough.

#### Question 9
**Correct answer:** B. Random assignment controls selection, so the groups differ only by chance. With no drop-out and the same measurement, the design supports the causal claim for these pupils.
**A:** Wrong. An experiment manipulates the intervention before the outcome is measured, so the direction is known. The direction problem belongs to correlational designs. It catches students who mix up experiments and correlational designs.
**C:** Wrong. Random assignment, not matching, is what controls selection. It catches students who think only deliberate matching makes groups comparable.
**D:** Wrong. A randomised trial supports causal claims best. Setting is a question of external validity and does not remove the causal claim for these pupils. It catches students who mix up internal and external validity.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** C. Random assignment supports the causal claim within the sample, but a sample from one private school is unrepresentative, so generalising to all pupils is not supported.
**A:** Wrong. Random assignment controls selection, which is about internal validity. It does not make a sample representative. It catches students who think random assignment secures external validity.
**B:** Wrong. Random assignment among the volunteers still creates equivalent groups. Volunteering limits generalisation, not the comparison between the two groups. It catches students who mix up selection into the study with selection into groups.
**D:** Wrong. A randomised design supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection. It catches students who doubt experiments for the wrong reason.

## Check against the blueprint

| Row | Planned | Written | Questions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | 4 | 4 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| R2 | 6 | 6 | 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 |
| Total | 10 questions, 10 points | 10 questions, 10 points | 1–10 |

Correct answers by position: A = 2 (questions 3, 7), B = 3 (questions 1, 6, 9), C = 3 (questions 4, 5, 10), D = 2 (questions 2, 8).

I saw no error in the blueprint. Notes on coverage:
- R1 uses instrumentation, regression to the mean, attrition and artificial setting as the correct answers.
- The other threats from the material (selection, history, maturation, testing, unrepresentative sample) appear as distractors or in R2.
- R2 covers the randomised controlled trial twice (9, 10), the quasi-experiment twice (7, 8), the one-group pretest–posttest once (5) and the correlational design once (6).
- Question 10 also touches external validity, which fits the evaluation of what an RCT does and does not support.

## Self-check

- **Does every multiple-choice question have exactly one correct answer?** Yes, each stem names a specific threat or design limit that the material settles, and each distractor is wrong under the material.
- **Is there no clue to the correct answer anywhere?** Yes, I balanced option lengths and form and spread the correct answers over A to D. Option C in question 10 is slightly longer because it has two parts, and the same-length options lessen that effect.
- **Are all distractors plausible?** Yes, each distractor is a real misconception, such as confusing internal and external validity, or reading a correlation as cause.
- **Does every question test the cognitive level of its row?** Yes. Questions 1–4 apply threat categories to new cases. Questions 5–10 judge whether a design can answer a causal question.
- **Does everything follow from the material?** Yes, all cases are new and fictitious and given in full, and all judgements follow from the threats and designs in the material.
- **Does any question give away the answer to another?** No, each case is self-contained and no question needs another's answer.

This is a draft. The teacher decides on the test.

### Stage: blueprint

## Koppeling met de leeruitkomsten

- **De student past de 4 P's toe op een gegeven product van een mkb-bedrijf.** Denkniveau: toepassen. Alle vragen horen bij een nieuwe casus (een ander product en bedrijf dan in de leerstof) en vragen om toepassing van product, prijs, plaats en promotie, inclusief hun samenhang. Er is geen lager denkniveau als voorwaarde opgenomen.
- **De student berekent de break-evenafzet bij gegeven vaste kosten, prijs en variabele kosten per stuk.** Denkniveau: toepassen (een bekende procedure uitvoeren in een nieuwe situatie). Alle vragen gebruiken andere getallen dan het voorbeeld in de leerstof (€ 12.000, € 25, € 10). De afleiders in de meerkeuzevragen zijn gebaseerd op de veelgemaakte fouten: delen door de prijs in plaats van door de dekkingsbijdrage, en vaste en variabele kosten verwisselen.
- **De student kent de begrippen van de marketingmix.** Niet opgenomen, zie "Niet opgenomen".

## Toetsmatrijs

| Rij | Leeruitkomst | Denkniveau | Vraagvorm | Aantal vragen | Punten per vraag | Punten |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | 4 P's toepassen | Toepassen | Meerkeuze | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| R2 | 4 P's toepassen | Toepassen | Open | 2 | 4 | 8 |
| R3 | Break-evenafzet berekenen | Toepassen | Meerkeuze | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| R4 | Break-evenafzet berekenen | Toepassen | Open | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| Totaal | | | | 10 | | 20 |

## Verdeling en punten

Het totaal van 20 punten komt van de docent. Weging, toetsduur en cesuur zijn niet opgegeven, dus daar is niets over vastgelegd.

| Leeruitkomst | Punten | Aandeel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 P's toepassen | 11 | 55% |
| Break-evenafzet berekenen | 9 | 45% |

- **Voorstel:** de verdeling van 5 vragen per leeruitkomst en de puntenverdeling hierboven. De eerste leeruitkomst weegt iets zwaarder omdat de student vier onderdelen en hun samenhang moet toepassen, terwijl de tweede één procedure vraagt.
- **Voorstel:** open vragen krijgen meer punten dan meerkeuzevragen. Bij R2 beoordeel je onderbouwing en samenhang tussen de P's. Bij R4 geef je deelpunten voor de juiste dekkingsbijdrage, de juiste formule en het juiste eindantwoord.

## Niet opgenomen

- **De student kent de begrippen van de marketingmix.** "Kent" is geen waarneembaar werkwoord, dus hier kunnen geen eenduidige vragen bij worden geschreven. De matrijs is gebouwd met de overige twee leeruitkomsten.
  - **Voorstel voor een herschreven leeruitkomst:** "De student benoemt de vier P's van de marketingmix en geeft per P een onderdeel." Dit toetst onthouden en is goed met meerkeuze te meten.
  - Pas de leeruitkomst aan in het formulier als je dit wilt overnemen. De matrijs wordt dan opnieuw opgesteld, waarbij de 10 vragen en 20 punten over drie leeruitkomsten verdeeld moeten worden.

## Zelfcheck

- **Telt de matrijs op?** Ja: 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10 vragen en 3 + 8 + 3 + 6 = 20 punten.
- **Toetst elke leeruitkomst op het denkniveau van het werkwoord?** Ja: "past toe" en "berekent" vragen toepassen, en alle rijen toetsen toepassen in een nieuwe casus.
- **Heeft elke opgenomen leeruitkomst minstens twee vragen?** Ja: elke opgenomen leeruitkomst heeft 5 vragen.
- **Past elke vraagvorm bij het denkniveau?** Ja: meerkeuze en open vragen kunnen beide toepassen meten, en er is geen leeruitkomst op creëren.

Dit is een concept. De docent stelt de toets vast.

### Stage: items

## Vragen

### Vraag 1 (1 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf maakt handgemaakte kaarsen en verkoopt die via een eigen webshop. De eigenaar overweegt vier besluiten. Welk besluit is een besluit over plaats?

A. De kaarsen ook verkopen in een cadeauwinkel in de stad
B. Een nieuwe geur toevoegen aan het assortiment van kaarsen
C. In december tien procent korting geven op alle kaarsen
D. Een influencer op Instagram de kaarsen laten tonen

### Vraag 2 (1 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf maakt handgemaakte bonbons in het premiumsegment, tegen een hoge prijs. De eigenaar wil dat de vier P's bij elkaar passen. Welk distributiekanaal past hierbij het best?

A. Verkopen via discountsupermarkten in de regio
B. Verkopen via de eigen webshop en enkele delicatessenzaken in de regio
C. Verkopen via tankstationshops in de regio
D. Verkopen via een groothandel voor alle soorten winkels

### Vraag 3 (1 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf maakt ambachtelijk houten speelgoed in het premiumsegment en verkoopt dit via enkele speelgoedboetieks. Welke prijskeuze past bij de overige P's?

A. Een prijs lager dan massaspeelgoed, zodat veel winkels het willen verkopen
B. Een prijs gelijk aan massaspeelgoed, zodat ouders niet hoeven te kiezen
C. Een prijs met steeds grote kortingen, zodat het speelgoed snel uitverkocht raakt
D. Een prijs hoger dan massaspeelgoed, zodat het product een exclusieve uitstraling houdt

### Vraag 4 (4 pt)
Atelier Van Dam is een mkb-bedrijf dat handgebouwde stadsfietsen in het premiumsegment gaat verkopen. De eigenaar wil een marketingmix waarin de vier P's bij elkaar passen.

Geef per P (product, prijs, plaats en promotie) één concrete keuze voor Atelier Van Dam. Leg bij elke keuze in één zin uit waarom die past bij de andere P's. Gebruik in totaal maximaal acht zinnen.

### Vraag 5 (4 pt)
Brander Bergmann is een mkb-bedrijf dat premium koffie van één herkomst verkoopt in een luxe blik van 250 gram. De eigenaar heeft deze marketingmix:

- Product: drie soorten koffie van hoge kwaliteit in een luxe blik.
- Prijs: lager dan de gangbare koffie in het schap.
- Plaats: discountsupermarkten door het hele land.
- Promotie: Instagram-berichten over het ambacht en de herkomst van de bonen.

Twee van de vier P's passen niet bij een premium product. Noem die twee P's. Leg per P in één zin uit waarom hij niet past en geef een passende aanpassing.

### Vraag 6 (1 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf maakt designlampen. De vaste kosten zijn € 18.000 per jaar. De verkoopprijs is € 30 per lamp en de variabele kosten zijn € 6 per lamp. Hoeveel lampen moet het bedrijf per jaar verkopen om break-even te draaien?

A. 500 lampen
B. 600 lampen
C. 750 lampen
D. 3.000 lampen

### Vraag 7 (1 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf maakt leren notitieboeken. De vaste kosten zijn € 9.600 per jaar. De verkoopprijs is € 20 per notitieboek en de variabele kosten zijn € 12 per notitieboek. Hoeveel notitieboeken moet het bedrijf per jaar verkopen om break-even te draaien?

A. 300 notitieboeken
B. 480 notitieboeken
C. 800 notitieboeken
D. 1.200 notitieboeken

### Vraag 8 (1 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf verkoopt verse sappen. De vaste kosten zijn € 2.400 per maand. De verkoopprijs is € 8 per fles en de variabele kosten zijn € 2 per fles. Hoeveel flessen moet het bedrijf per maand verkopen om break-even te draaien?

A. 240 flessen
B. 300 flessen
C. 400 flessen
D. 1.200 flessen

### Vraag 9 (3 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf verkoopt tuinverlichting. De vaste kosten zijn € 15.000 per jaar. De verkoopprijs is € 40 per stuk en de variabele kosten zijn € 15 per stuk.

Bereken de break-evenafzet per jaar. Geef de dekkingsbijdrage per stuk, de formule en het eindantwoord, met de berekening erbij.

### Vraag 10 (3 pt)
Een mkb-bedrijf exploiteert een foodtruck met smoothies. De vaste kosten zijn € 5.400 per maand. De verkoopprijs is € 9 per smoothie en de variabele kosten zijn € 3 per smoothie.

Bereken de break-evenafzet per maand. Geef de dekkingsbijdrage per smoothie, de formule en het eindantwoord, met de berekening erbij.

## Antwoordmodel

### Rij R1 — toepassen (vraag 1–3)

#### Vraag 1
**Goed antwoord:** A. Verkopen in een cadeauwinkel gaat over het distributiekanaal en de locatie, en die horen bij plaats.
- **B:** Fout, een nieuwe geur is een wijziging in het assortiment en hoort bij product. De afleider vangt de verwarring tussen assortiment (product) en distributie (plaats).
- **C:** Fout, een kortingsactie is een besluit over kortingen en hoort bij prijs. De afleider vangt de verwarring tussen een actie in de winkel en de keuze van het verkoopkanaal.
- **D:** Fout, samenwerken met een influencer op Instagram is social media en hoort bij promotie. De afleider vangt de misvatting dat een online kanaal altijd plaats is, terwijl dit hier om communicatie gaat.

#### Vraag 2
**Goed antwoord:** B. Een premium product vraagt volgens de leerstof selectieve distributie, en een eigen webshop met enkele delicatessenzaken is selectief.

### Stage: items

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
A Grade 4 teacher starts a lesson on fractions. Which way of starting applies the principle of review?

A. She states the lesson goal and immediately shows the first new fraction example.
B. She has pupils answer a few quick questions about the fractions from the previous lesson.
C. She spends the first twenty minutes re-teaching the whole previous unit.
D. She hands out a worksheet with new fraction sums for pupils to do alone.

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A Grade 3 teacher is teaching how to tell time: full hours, half hours and quarter hours. Which lesson build presents the material in small steps?

A. She explains full, half and quarter hours in one explanation, then pupils practise all three.
B. She lets pupils practise with all clock times on their own first, then explains afterwards.
C. She explains full hours and moves straight on to half and quarter hours, because the first step was easy.
D. She explains full hours and lets pupils practise them, then explains half hours and lets pupils practise those.

### Question 3 (1 pt)
A teacher has just shown how to round numbers to the nearest ten. Which action checks the understanding of all pupils?

A. She gives every pupil a rounding problem to solve on a mini-whiteboard and looks at all the answers.
B. She asks, "Does everyone understand?" and continues if nobody says no.
C. She asks one pupil who raised a hand to explain the rule and continues if that answer is correct.
D. She asks pupils to hold up a thumb if they think they understand and continues if most thumbs are up.

### Question 4 (1 pt)
A teacher has just shown how to solve a word problem. Which situation is guided practice?

A. Pupils watch while the teacher solves another word problem on the board.
B. Pupils solve a set of word problems alone, and the teacher marks them afterwards.
C. Pupils solve a word problem step by step with the teacher, who prompts them and corrects mistakes on the spot.
D. Pupils take word problems home as homework.

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A teacher in a class of 20 pupils asks all pupils to solve one practice problem on their mini-whiteboards. 12 pupils answer correctly. The teacher had planned to continue with independent practice. What should the teacher conclude and do?

A. Most pupils got it right, so she continues with independent practice and the others will catch up.
B. The success rate is 60%, which is below the aim of about 80%, so she gives more guided practice before moving on.
C. 12 out of 20 is about 80%, so she continues with independent practice.
D. A success rate of 60% is fine, because 100% would mean the task is too easy, so she continues as planned.

### Question 6 (1 pt)
Grade 5 pupils get stuck when writing an argumentative text. The teacher gives each pupil a card with sentence starters and a step-by-step list to use while writing. Which principle of direct instruction does this apply?

A. Review previous learning
B. Check for understanding
C. Require independent practice
D. Provide scaffolds

### Question 7 (1 pt)
According to the course, besides the short review at the start of a lesson, how often should students be engaged in review?

A. Daily and weekly
B. Daily and monthly
C. Weekly and monthly
D. Monthly and yearly

### Question 8 (1 pt)
Which statement is a common misconception about direct instruction?

A. Direct instruction means that the teacher lectures without interaction.
B. Direct instruction includes providing models and worked examples.
C. Direct instruction includes monitoring independent practice.
D. Direct instruction includes presenting new material in small steps.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Understand (questions 1–6)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. A few quick questions about the previous lesson is a short review of previous learning at the start of the lesson.
- **A:** This skips the review and goes straight to new material. It catches students who think a lesson starts with the goal and new content.
- **C:** Twenty minutes re-teaching a whole unit is not a *short* review. It catches students who confuse review with re-teaching.
- **D:** This is new material, practised alone, with no review. It catches students who confuse the start of the lesson with independent practice.

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** D. The teacher presents one small step and pupils practise it before the next step is presented.
- **A:** This is one large step with practice only at the end. It catches students who think a clear explanation is enough without practice after each step.
- **B:** Practice comes before the explanation, so the new material is not presented in steps. It catches a mix-up of the order of presenting and practising.
- **C:** This moves on without practice after the first step. It catches students who treat "small steps" as only splitting up the explanation, with no practice in between.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. Every pupil gives a response to a concrete problem and the teacher checks all responses.
- **B:** This is the misconception that checking for understanding means asking "Does everyone understand?". Pupils who do not understand often stay silent.
- **C:** This checks only one pupil, and one who volunteered. It catches students who think one correct answer shows that the class understands.
- **D:** This asks pupils for their own impression instead of a response to a question. It is a variant of the misconception in B.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. The teacher and pupils practise together, with prompts and immediate correction, which is guided practice.
- **A:** This is modelling by the teacher, and the pupils do not practise. It catches a mix-up of modelling and guided practice.
- **B:** The pupils work alone and are corrected afterwards. This is independent practice. It catches the misconception that guided practice is the same as independent practice.
- **D:** Homework is independent practice without the teacher present. It catches the same misconception as B.

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** B. 12 out of 20 is 60%, which is below the aim of about 80%, so more guided practice is needed before moving on.
- **A:** A majority is not enough. The aim is a high success rate of about 80%. It catches students who accept "most pupils" as enough.
- **C:** This is a calculation error: 12 out of 20 is 60%, not 80% (16 out of 20 would be 80%).
- **D:** This ignores the aim of about 80% and turns a low success rate into a virtue. It catches students who think more errors always mean more learning.

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** D. A card with sentence starters and a step-by-step list is a scaffold for a task the pupils find hard.
- **A:** No earlier learning is reviewed. It catches students who pick the first principle in the list.
- **B:** The card supports the pupils during the task. It does not check what they understand. It catches a mix-up of support and checking.
- **C:** The pupils do write alone, but the principle shown is the support they get. It catches students who look only at the work form.

### Row R2 — Remember (questions 7–8)

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** C. The material names weekly and monthly review.
- **A:** "Daily" is not part of this principle (the start-of-lesson review is the daily element). Stopping at weekly misses the monthly review.
- **B:** This combines a correct element ("monthly") with a wrong one ("daily"). It catches students who remember the rhythm only partly.
- **D:** The intervals are too long. It catches students who think review is only needed after long gaps.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** A. This is the first common misconception named in the material. Direct instruction includes asking many questions and checking responses, so it is not lecturing without interaction.
- **B:** Providing models and worked examples is a principle of direct instruction, so it is correct and not a misconception.
- **C:** Requiring and monitoring independent practice is a principle of direct instruction, so it is correct and not a misconception.

### Stage: blueprint

## Link to the learning outcomes

- **Outcome 1: The student explains the principles of direct instruction using classroom examples.** The verb "explains" is the cognitive process **Understand**. Some questions test **Remember** as a prerequisite: the student must know the five principles (review, small steps, guided practice, checking for understanding, independent practice) and the related terms before being able to explain them.
- **Outcome 2: The student designs a lesson plan for a primary school group that applies the principles of direct instruction.** The verb "designs" is the cognitive process **Create**. It cannot be measured with multiple choice (see "Not included").

## Test blueprint

| Row | Learning outcome | Cognitive level | Question type | Number of questions | Points per question | Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Explain principles of direct instruction with classroom examples | Understand | Multiple choice | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| R2 | Explain principles of direct instruction with classroom examples (prerequisite: knowing the five principles and key terms) | Remember | Multiple choice | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| Total | | | | 8 | | 8 |

Notes for step 2:
- **R1** uses classroom examples. Questions can ask the student to explain why a teacher action fits or does not fit a principle, to distinguish guided from independent practice, to interpret what an effective check for understanding looks like, and to refute the listed misconceptions (lecturing without interaction, guided practice as independent practice, "Does everyone understand?"). Cover all five principles across the six questions.
- **R2** asks only for recall of the five principles and the terms used in the material, such as the success rate of about 80% and scaffolds. Do not go beyond the material.

## Distribution and points

- **Outcome 1 (explain principles):** 8 of 8 questions, 8 of 8 points, 100% of the test. Within it, Understand carries 6 points (75%) and the Remember prerequisite carries 2 points (25%).
- **Outcome 2 (design a lesson plan):** 0 points, 0%. It is not part of this test (see "Not included").
- **Points per question:** Proposal: 1 point per question, 8 points in total. The teacher gave no points.
- **Distribution:** Proposal: because only one outcome can be tested in this format, all questions go to it, with most at the level of the verb (Understand).
- **Test duration:** not given, so no time check was made.
- **Pass mark and weighting:** not given by the teacher, so none is proposed here.

## Not included

- **Outcome 2: The student designs a lesson plan for a primary school group that applies the principles of direct instruction.**
  - **Why:** "Designs" is Create. The student has to produce a lesson plan, and a multiple-choice question can only have them select an existing option. The teacher asked for multiple choice only, so I wrote no make-believe questions for this outcome.
  - **What fits instead:** a product assessment. The student hands in a lesson plan for a primary school group, assessed with a rubric whose criteria follow the principles of direct instruction (review, small steps, guided practice, checking for understanding, independent practice). If the teacher allows open questions, a short case-based open question could cover part of the outcome, but a complete lesson plan is better assessed as a separate assignment.
  - **Consequence for the test:** with this outcome removed, the test covers only half of the learning outcomes. The teacher may want to account for this in the course's overall assessment plan.

### Stage: items

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
A group 5 teacher starts every maths lesson with five minutes of short questions on the previous lesson, for example yesterday's work on fractions. Only after that does she present the new material. Which explanation best shows why this fits direct instruction?

A. It lets the teacher check the previous lesson so the results can go into the report.
B. It brings earlier learning back to mind so the new material can connect to it.
C. It replaces a separate explanation, so the teacher saves time for practice.
D. It lets students who missed the previous lesson catch up on everything.

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A group 6 teacher teaches written long division. Which lesson sequence applies the principle of small steps?

A. She explains the whole procedure with one example, then students do a worksheet of ten sums.
B. She hands out a written explanation of the procedure, then students practise in pairs.
C. She demonstrates all steps in one go, then asks students to repeat the steps back to her.
D. She teaches one step, students practise that step, then she adds the next step and they practise again.

### Question 3 (1 pt)
A group 3 teacher wants students to practise adding up to 100. Which situation is guided practice and not independent practice?

A. Students solve a sum on mini whiteboards while the teacher watches, gives prompts and corrects errors at once.
B. Students complete a worksheet alone and in silence while the teacher marks the previous test.
C. Students take ten sums home and hand them in the next day for the teacher to mark.
D. Students watch the teacher solve three sums on the board and copy her answers in their notebooks.

### Question 4 (1 pt)
After explaining a new spelling rule, a teacher asks, "Does everyone understand?" Nobody says anything, so she moves on. Which change turns this into an effective check for understanding?

A. She asks the same question again, more slowly, and waits until students respond.
B. She asks the students who do not understand to raise their hands.
C. She gives a short exercise and has all students show their answers on mini whiteboards.
D. She asks the best student in the group to explain the rule to the others.

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A colleague says: "Direct instruction means that the teacher lectures and the students only listen." Which reply is correct according to the course?

A. "That is correct: interaction only begins during independent practice at the end of the lesson."
B. "That is incorrect: the teacher asks many questions, checks the responses of all students and guides practice."
C. "That is correct, but only for new topics; interaction is saved for the review of old topics."
D. "That is incorrect: the teacher does not present anything, and students work out the new material themselves."

### Question 6 (1 pt)
In group 7, students practise calculating percentages independently. The teacher checks the work and sees that only about half of the students answered the tasks correctly. Which conclusion and action fit best with direct instruction?

A. The tasks were challenging in a good way, so she moves on to the next step.
B. The students need more independent practice, so she hands out a second worksheet.
C. A few students lacked effort, so she sets the remaining tasks as homework.
D. The success rate is too low, so she goes back to guided practice or adds scaffolds.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
Which of the following is a principle of direct instruction as taught in this course?

A. Engaging students in weekly and monthly review.
B. Letting students discover new material on their own before any explanation.
C. Dividing students into fixed ability groups for the whole lesson.
D. Grading every practice task so the marks count toward the report.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
According to the course, which success rate should students reach during practice?

A. About 60%
B. About 70%
C. About 80%
D. About 90%

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Understand (questions 1–6)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. A short review of previous learning activates prior knowledge, so the new material can be linked to it.
**A:** The review is not a test for the report. This catches the mix-up of review with grading.
**C:** The review does not replace presenting new material. The new material is still presented in small steps. This catches the idea that review is a time-saving substitute for instruction.
**D:** The review is short and meant for all students. It is not a catch-up session for absent students. This catches the mix-up of a short review with reteaching.

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** D. The new material is presented in small steps, with practice after each step.
**A:** The whole procedure is presented at once, and practice comes only at the end. This catches the idea that one good example is enough.
**B:** The material is given at once in written form, and there is no practice after each step. This catches the idea that clear written material equals small steps.
**C:** All steps are demonstrated at once. Repeating them back is not practice after each step. This catches the idea that checking at the end replaces small steps.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. In guided practice the teacher is present, prompts, and corrects students while they practise.
**B:** Students work alone and the teacher does not monitor, which is independent practice. This catches the misconception that guided and independent practice are the same.
**C:** Homework is independent practice. This catches the same misconception.
**D:** The teacher is modelling and the students are not practising yet. This catches the mix-up of a model or worked example with guided practice.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. All students respond at the same time, so the teacher sees every response and can decide whether to move on.
**A:** It is still the same self-report question, only slower. This catches the misconception that "Does everyone understand?" is a check.
**B:** Students who do not understand often do not raise their hands, and the teacher does not see all responses. This catches the same misconception in another form.
**D:** One strong student does not show the understanding of the others. This catches the idea that one correct answer means the group understands.

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** B. Direct instruction includes many questions, checking the responses of all students, and guided practice.
**A:** Interaction is present throughout the lesson, not only at the end. This partly accepts the misconception.
**C:** This also accepts the misconception and wrongly limits interaction to review.
**D:** The teacher does present the material, with models and worked examples. This catches the mix-up of rejecting the misconception while describing discovery learning.

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** D. A success rate that is far below the aimed-for high rate means the students are not ready for independent work. The teacher goes back to guided practice or adds scaffolds.
**A:** Moving on at a low success rate leaves students without mastery. This catches the idea that struggling is always productive.
**B:** More independent practice at a low success rate lets students keep making errors. This catches the idea that more practice alone solves the problem.
**C:** This blames effort without evidence and does not respond to the result. This catches the idea that a low result means lack of motivation.

### Row R2 — Remember (questions 7–8)

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** A. Engaging students in weekly and monthly review is one of the principles in the material.
**B:** Direct instruction presents new material in small steps, with models and worked examples. This catches the mix-up with discovery learning.
**C:** Fixed ability grouping is not a principle in the material. This catches a general belief about differentiation.
**D:** The material asks for monitoring independent practice, not grading every task for the report. This catches the mix-up of monitoring with marking.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** C. The material states that a high success rate of about 80% is the aim.
**A:** 60% is too low. This catches a misremembered figure.
**B:** 70% is too low. This catches a misremembered figure.
**D:** 90% is higher than the figure in the material. This catches the idea that a higher figure is always better.

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
A colleague watches a lesson in which the teacher explains a new concept in small steps. After each step she asks questions and all students show their answers on mini whiteboards. The colleague says: "This is not direct instruction. Direct instruction means lecturing." Which statement is correct?

B. The colleague is wrong, because direct instruction includes presenting in small steps and asking many questions to which all students respond.
C. The colleague is wrong, because in direct instruction students mainly work alone and the teacher explains only briefly at the start.

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A teacher shows a worked example of adding fractions. Then she gives the class ten similar sums. The students work silently on their own while she sits at her desk and marks books. She says: "This is my guided practice." Which statement is correct?

A. It is guided practice, because the students practise directly after the worked example.
B. It is guided practice, because the sums match the content of the explanation.
C. It is a review, because the students repeat the content of the explanation.
D. It is independent practice, because the students work alone, without support or feedback during the task.

### Question 3 (1 pt)
After explaining one step of a spelling rule, a teacher asks: "Does everyone understand?" No one raises a hand, so she moves on to the next step. Why is this a weak way of checking for understanding?

A. Silence does not show understanding; a good check makes all students give a response, for example by writing an answer on a whiteboard.
B. The question is fine, but it should be asked after the independent practice instead of after each step.
C. The question is too difficult; a good check asks only the strongest students to explain the rule to the others.
D. The question is a good check, but only if the teacher waits longer for raised hands before she moves on.

### Question 4 (1 pt)
A teacher explains all five steps of long division in one 15-minute presentation. Only then do the students start to practise. Many students make errors in the first steps. Which explanation fits direct instruction?

A. She should have started with a longer review of last week's lesson, so that errors in the first steps do not occur.
B. She should have let students practise alone for longer before the explanation, so that they discover the steps themselves.
C. She should have presented one step, let students practise it, and then presented the next step, so that errors are noticed early.
D. She should have repeated the whole procedure a week later in a weekly review, so that the errors disappear.

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A teacher starts a lesson on multiplication with five minutes of quick questions about the tables from the previous lesson. A student teacher says: "That is a waste of time. The lesson should only contain new material." Which statement explains why the teacher's action fits direct instruction?

A. It fits, because review belongs only at the start of a week or month, so a short review before new material is useful as an extra.
B. It fits, because a short review of previous learning prepares students for the new material and shows the teacher what needs repeating.
C. It fits, because the review replaces the need to check for understanding during the rest of the lesson.
D. It fits, because the quick questions are independent practice that students do at the start of the lesson.

A. The check shows that almost all students can do the task, so they can practise alone while she monitors their work.
B. Independent practice replaces guided practice once the explanation is finished, so the check on the whiteboards was not needed.
C. During independent practice the teacher should stay away, so students learn to work without any help.
D. Students should have practised alone before the check, because a check belongs at the end of the independent practice.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
According to the principles of instruction in this course, what success rate should students reach during practice?

A. About 40%
B. About 60%
C. About 80%
D. About 100%

### Question 8 (1 pt)
In the principles of instruction in this course, which of these is done in weekly and monthly moments?

A. Checking the responses of all students on new material
B. Providing scaffolds for difficult tasks
C. Requiring and monitoring independent practice
D. Engaging students in review of earlier learning

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Understand (questions 1–6)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. Direct instruction is interactive: new material is presented in small steps, and many questions are asked and the responses of all students are checked.
**A:** Wrong. This is the misconception that direct instruction means lecturing without interaction. In the material, questions are asked throughout the lesson.
**C:** Wrong. It mixes up direct instruction with independent work. Independent practice is one principle, but the teacher also explains, models and guides throughout.
**D:** Wrong. Checking the responses of all students is itself one of Rosenshine's principles. The distractor catches students who do not see questioning as part of the approach.

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** D. The students work alone without support or feedback, which is independent practice. Guided practice is practice with the teacher's support and feedback.
**A:** Wrong. Practising right after the explanation does not make it guided. This distractor catches the misconception that guided practice is the same as independent practice.
**B:** Wrong. Matching the sums to the explanation is true of both forms of practice, so it does not decide the type. It catches students who judge by content, not by teacher support.
**C:** Wrong. A review returns to previous learning; these sums practise the new material. It catches a mix-up of review and practice.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. "Does everyone understand?" gives no evidence, because silent students may not understand or may not realise it. A check must make all students show a response.
**B:** Wrong. Understanding must be checked before moving on, after the steps, not only after independent practice.
**C:** Wrong. Asking only the strongest students gives no information about the others. The material says to check the responses of all students.
**D:** Wrong. Waiting longer does not fix the problem. The question itself still gives no response from all students. It catches students who think the question only needs better timing.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. Present new material in small steps with practice after each step, so errors are noticed and corrected before the next step.
**A:** Wrong. A review comes at the start and activates previous learning. It does not solve errors that arise from a long presentation.
**B:** Wrong. Practising alone before the explanation is not part of the principles. Practice follows the presentation of each small step, with guidance.
**D:** Wrong. Weekly review strengthens learning over time but does not prevent errors during the lesson. It catches students who mix up review with the lesson structure.

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** B. A short review of previous learning at the start prepares for new material and shows what needs repeating.
**A:** Wrong. Weekly and monthly review is a separate principle. The first principle is a short review at the start of each lesson, not only an extra.
**C:** Wrong. Review does not replace checking for understanding. These are separate principles, and checking continues throughout the lesson.
**D:** Wrong. Quick questions on previous learning are a review, not independent practice. It catches a mix-up of principles.

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** A. The check showed that nearly all students succeed, so they are ready to practise alone, and the teacher monitors the practice.
**B:** Wrong. Checking for understanding comes before moving on. Skipping it mixes up guided and independent practice.
**C:** Wrong. The material says to require and monitor independent practice, so walking around is part of it.
**D:** Wrong. The check comes before the move to independent practice. This catches a mix-up of the order of the principles.

### Row R2 — Remember (questions 7–8)

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** C. The material says to obtain a high success rate of about 80%.
**A:** Wrong. 40% is far too low, and students would be mostly failing. It is the least plausible distractor but may be chosen by students who do not remember the figure.
**B:** Wrong. 60% is too low, and many students would still be struggling. It catches students who guess a "pass" level.
**D:** Wrong. 100% is not the aim in the material. It catches the common idea that practice should be errorless.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** D. Engaging students in weekly and monthly review is a principle in the material.
**A:** Wrong. Checking the responses of all students happens during the lesson. It is not tied to weekly and monthly moments.
**B:** Wrong. Scaffolds are for difficult tasks, not for a time interval.
**C:** Wrong. Independent practice is required and monitored in the lesson. It is not the weekly and monthly principle.

De collega gebruikt D0 in plaats van D1, de juiste waarde is €37,08. 4. Bij een koers onder €37,08. 5. D1 = €1,89, W0 = 1,89 / 0,03 = €63,00: veel hoger, omdat k − g kleiner wordt.
